answers.answer: Redis is a server (a TCP daemon) that manipulates abstract data types held in a key space; keys are binary-safe strings and values are types such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and vector sets (plus module types such as JSON, time series, probabilistic filters and the Query Engine). Data is kept primarily in memory (the main goal remains an in-memory database), with optional copies to disk (RDB snapshots, AOF) and to replicas. The README addresses developers building real-time data-driven applications and lists use cases: caching, session management, querying/sorting/analytics, messaging and interservice communication, and vector operations; per type: caching/counters, representing objects, stacks and queues, unique-item tracking and set algebra, leaderboards and rate limiters, event sourcing/sensor monitoring/notifications, semantic similarity search and RAG.
answers.where: index.md intro, Core ideas (six ideas, data type table), Advantages the maintainers state; understanding.md Purpose/Beneficiary

answers.answer: RDB snapshots dump the whole data set to disk (forked child runs rdbSave, triggered by save points in serverCron or BGSAVE); the AOF logs every write command. Durability: with default snapshotting a crash or power outage can lose a few minutes of writes (depending on save points); with the AOF and default everysec fsync about one second of writes (or a single write if only the process fails), always is safest/slowest, no lets the OS flush. Both can be on at once. At startup loadDataFromDisk loads the AOF (loadAppendOnlyFiles) when the AOF is enabled, otherwise the RDB (rdbLoad); a preload-file setting overrides both.
answers.where: index.md Core ideas 'Disk is an optional copy', Workflow 3, Trade-offs (Durability, appendfsync table)

answers.answer: The background jobs service (src/bio.c) uses worker threads to do background close(2), AOF fsync and lazy freeing (e.g. UNLINK, freeObjAsync above LAZYFREE_THRESHOLD of 64), taking that blocking work off the main thread. Its ordering guarantee: not stated.

answers.answer: Modules are shared libraries loaded into redis-server to extend Redis and rapidly implement new commands (JSON, search, time series, probabilistic come as pinned external modules in modules/modules.yaml; vector sets are an in-tree module). A loadmodule line in the configuration reaches queueLoadModule at startup, and main calls moduleLoadFromQueue (outside Sentinel mode); bundled modules are fetched with make modules-update and configured through the generated redis-full.conf. How a module registers commands is not traced (src/module.c excluded). Whether a module can be loaded into an already running server (e.g. by a command) is not stated beyond enable-module-command being blocked by default. How a module's own data type is saved and restored: not stated.
answers.where: index.md Workflow 6, Mechanisms table (Modules row), Settings table; glossary 'module'

answers.answer: The event loop (src/ae.c) runs aeMain, which repeatedly calls aeProcessEvents: it calls beforeSleep, waits for readiness with aeApiPoll (backed by evport, epoll, kqueue or select), calls afterSleep, then runs ready file events (read handler first, write handler second unless AE_BARRIER inverts it) and time events such as serverCron (run server.hz times per second: active expiry, rehashing, starting saves, replication reconnection). The connection layer (connSocketAcceptHandler in socket.c) accepts sockets and passes them to acceptCommonHandler in networking.c, which applies maxclients and calls createClient, installing readQueryFromClient as the read handler; reads feed processInputBuffer, which parses and dispatches to processCommand in server.c. beforeSleep flushes the AOF (flushAppendOnlyFile) and then sends pending replies (handleClientsWithPendingWrites). Optional I/O threads read/parse/write but hand commands to the main thread.
answers.where: index.md Workflow 2, Mechanisms figure and table; deep-dives/mechanism-deep-dive.md

answers.answer: Not stated: the artifact does not describe the containers holding keys and expirations, how they change in cluster mode, or where a key's name is stored relative to its value. It only says a cluster splits keys across nodes by hash slot, and that the robj holds a value's type, encoding, LRU/LFU data, refcount and payload pointer.

answers.answer: The type is what a value is (an abstract version of a fundamental data structure, e.g. a list, defined by its operations and their complexity); the encoding is how it is represented in memory at the moment (e.g. strings RAW/EMBSTR/INT, sets INTSET/HT, small hashes/sets/zsets as listpack, lists as QUICKLIST of listpacks, streams as radix tree of listpacks). Both exist so memory-saving compact encodings can sit under each type; robj records both. Small values use compact forms until thresholds set in configuration (hash-max-listpack-entries/value, set-max-intset-entries, set-max-listpack-entries, zset-max-listpack-entries) are passed. Which code decides the conversion: not stated.
answers.where: glossary data-type/encoding; deep-dives/mechanism-deep-dive.md (encodings); index.md Mechanisms table

answers.answer: Clustering lives in src/cluster.c and src/cluster_legacy.c: together they map keys to slots, route requests and handle node failure (failure detection markNodeAsFailingIfNeeded and replica failover clusterHandleSlaveFailover / clusterFailoverReplaceYourMaster are cited; exact division between the files is not stated). keyHashSlot takes the low 14 bits of crc16 of the key (16384 slots), hashing only the {...} hash-tag part if present. processCommand calls getNodeByQuery to find the node serving the slot; if it is this node the command runs, otherwise clusterRedirectClient replies MOVED (or ASK during migration) with slot and address. Keys in different slots get -CROSSSLOT; multi-key requests during migration can get -TRYAGAIN.
answers.where: index.md Workflow 5, routing figure, Mechanisms table (Cluster), Trade-offs Distribution; glossary hash-slot

answers.answer: connSocketAcceptHandler accepts; acceptCommonHandler rejects if maxclients reached, else createClient installs readQueryFromClient; clientAcceptHandler refuses non-loopback clients in protected mode with no default password. On readability, readQueryFromClient reads into querybuf and calls processInputBuffer, which parses multibulk (*) or inline and (on main thread) calls processCommandAndResetClient -> processCommand (I/O threads only queue the client). processCommand looks up the command and gates it, then call runs c->cmd->proc (setCommand -> setGenericCommand -> setKeyByLink, server.dirty++, shared.ok reply). Since dirty changed, call queues the command via alsoPropagate (server.also_propagate, wrapped in MULTI/EXEC if several), propagateNow feeds feedAppendOnlyFile (into aof_buf) and replicationFeedSlaves. In beforeSleep, flushAppendOnlyFile writes (and with appendfsync always fsyncs) before handleClientsWithPendingWrites/writeToClient sends the reply. Checks that can stop it: authentication (noautherr), ACL (ACLCheckAllPerm, -NOPERM), cluster routing (redirect), memory (performEvictions fails and command deny-on-memory-limit -> OOM), disk errors (writeCommandsDeniedByDiskError), read-only replica (roslaveerr), loading (loadingerr); plus maxclients and protected mode at admission.
answers.where: index.md Workflow 2 and 'Main checks in processCommand' table; deep-dive (propagation)

answers.answer: When the AOF grows past auto-aof-rewrite-percentage and auto-aof-rewrite-min-size, serverCron calls rewriteAppendOnlyFileBackground, which forks a child. A manifest file names which files are current: at most one BASE (snapshot from the last rewrite, RDB format preferred), one or more ordered INCR files (writes since the last successful rewrite), and after a rewrite the old BASE and INCR become HISTORY files, removed automatically unless GC is disabled. The detailed step-by-step of the rewrite (how the child writes, how the parent switches INCR files and updates the manifest during it) is not stated.
answers.where: index.md Workflow 3, AOF lifecycle figure; deep-dive AOF lifecycle

answers.answer: replicationCron calls connectWithMaster, installing syncWithMaster, which via slaveTryPartialResynchronization sends PSYNC with a replication ID and offset. On the master, syncCommand calls masterTryPartialResynchronization: if the ID matches and the offset is still within the replication backlog it answers +CONTINUE and sends only the missing part. Otherwise it answers +FULLRESYNC, runs startBgsaveForReplication, and the replica receives the RDB in readSyncBulkPayload. Afterwards replicationFeedSlaves streams writes (a replica relays its master's stream unchanged to its own replicas). Diskless loading from the socket can only flush the old dataset after the new one is fully loaded (more memory) and risks data loss on failover.
answers.where: index.md Workflow 4, replica figure, Trade-offs Replication

answers.answer: Two mechanisms: on access, expireIfNeeded deletes an expired key on a master (a replica waits for the master's deletion); in the background, activeExpireCycle (run from serverCron) scans for expired keys. How the background cycle limits its cost: not stated. Consistency: replicas do not expire keys themselves; the master sends synthesized DEL operations; replication and the AOF share one propagation feed (so the AOF receiving the DEL is implied, not stated explicitly).
answers.where: deep-dive (Keys leave memory; propagation); index.md Mechanisms table (Key expiry, Periodic work)

answers.answer: LRU, LFU and minimal-TTL algorithms are approximated in order to save memory. The approximation samples keys (maxmemory-samples): the default of 5 gives good enough results, 10 approximates true LRU very closely but costs more CPU; you tune speed vs accuracy. Cost: imprecise victim selection, or more CPU for accuracy. Details of the sampling algorithm (e.g. eviction pool) are not stated.
answers.where: index.md Trade-offs, Memory

answers.answer: Not stated: the artifact only says serverCron's jobs include rehashing; it gives no rationale for incremental resizing or for discouraging resizing during a child save/rewrite, nor their costs (it only notes a forked child adds copy-on-write memory pressure).

answers.answer: The manifesto chooses a mostly single-threaded core and scales by presenting many cores (on one or many machines) as one system via Redis Cluster; shared-nothing is simpler and optimal in NUMA systems. Extra threads: I/O threads (io-threads, default 1) for socket reads, writes and protocol parsing, but only the main thread executes commands, and pub/sub, monitor, blocked and tracking clients stay on the main thread; bio worker threads for close(2), AOF fsync and lazy freeing; plus forked child processes for RDB saves and AOF rewrites. Stated costs/conditions: use threaded I/O only if you have performance problems with high CPU use; TLS.md says multi-threaded I/O is not supported for TLS (possibly stale); helper threads start after modules load because of an ld.so TLS/dlopen race; lazy free only above a 64 threshold; one slow command (big aggregate deletes, long scripts) blocks everything.
answers.where: index.md Core ideas, Trade-offs Single-threaded execution; deep-dive threads; understanding u-choice-1

answers.answer: appendfsync: always (fsync every write, slow, safest; a failed write exits the process since replies cannot be rolled back), everysec (default, compromise, lose ~1 second), no (OS flushes, fastest). The log is flushed in beforeSleep before replies are sent so that with always the write reaches the file before the reply goes out (AE_BARRIER supports fsync before replying); a batching/performance rationale is not stated. With no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes, up to 30 seconds of log can be lost in the worst case with default Linux settings.
answers.where: index.md Trade-offs (Durability, appendfsync table), Workflow 2 Flush; deep-dive AE_BARRIER

answers.answer: With maxmemory set, processCommand calls performEvictions before each command; it frees keys per maxmemory-policy. If it cannot free memory (default noeviction policy, or no key qualifies), commands marked deny-on-memory-limit / needing more memory get an OOM error while read-only commands like GET keep working. Not counted as you might expect: replica output buffers (set a lower maxmemory when replicas attached, unless noeviction), and forked-child copy-on-write memory adds pressure. A 32-bit instance with no limit gets 3 GB with noeviction. Whether replicas ignore maxmemory: not stated.
answers.where: index.md Trade-offs Memory, memory-limit figure, Main checks table

answers.answer: Failed background snapshot: with stop-writes-on-bgsave-error, writes are refused (writeCommandsDeniedByDiskError) so the operator notices. AOF write failure with appendfsync always: the process exits. Restoring via preload-file: startup aborts if the target is missing or cannot be loaded. Damaged AOF at startup and an unloadable RDB in normal loading: not stated.
answers.where: index.md Trade-offs Durability, Main checks table, Workflow 3

answers.answer: Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost; min-replicas-to-write (with a lag bound) makes the master stop accepting writes if not enough replicas are connected, limiting the exposure window but not guaranteeing N replicas accept the write. Diskless replica loading may cause data loss during failovers. Replicas are read-only to normal clients' writes. How a replica serves clients while its link to the master is down: not stated.
answers.where: index.md Trade-offs Replication, Main checks table

answers.answer: Multi-key commands must have all keys in one hash slot (else -CROSSSLOT; hash tags {...} help) and may get -TRYAGAIN during slot migration; a normal instance cannot join a cluster (needs cluster-enabled yes). Restrictions on databases: not stated. With uncovered hash slots, by default the whole cluster eventually becomes unavailable; cluster-require-full-coverage changes this.
